record.paper_title: A modified star formation law as a solution to open problems in galaxy evolution
record.context_brief: Baryonic recipes versus cosmology in galaxy clustering
record.original_question: When semi-analytic galaxy-formation models fail to match observed galaxy two-point auto-correlation functions, is the mismatch primarily caused by the baryonic recipes used to assign stellar masses and galaxy properties, or by the underlying cosmology of the dark-matter simulation? The issue is nontrivial because galaxy positions are tied to haloes and subhaloes, while stellar-mass selection and clustering predictions can change substantially when the star-formation law changes, and similar clustering matches can be obtained with different cosmological parameters depending on the baryonic recipes.

evidence.quote:
The two point auto-correlation function of galaxies is a fun -
damental measure of the spatial distribution of a certain
population of galaxies and is well determined by observa-
tions (e.g. Li et al. 2006). It is however not well ﬁtted by
current SAMs.

Thus, it is in general very hard to say
whether a mismatch with observed correlation functions in-
dicates a problem with baryonic recipes, or with cosmology.

We thus conﬁrm the results by Wang et al. (2008) who ﬁnd
that a similar match to observed correlation functions can b e
obtained by SAMs using diﬀerent cosmological parameters,
depending on the detailed baryonic recipes.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider semi-analytic models (SAMs) of galaxy formation built on top of a cosmological N-body simulation of dark matter. Such a model takes as input (i) a set of cosmological parameters Θ (e.g. Ω_m, Ω_Λ, σ_8, h, n_s) that determine the dark-matter merger trees and the spatial distribution of haloes and subhaloes, and (ii) a collection of "baryonic recipes" R (prescriptions for gas cooling, star formation, supernova and AGN feedback, mergers, and stellar evolution) that assign stellar masses and other observable properties to galaxies hosted by haloes/subhaloes. From (Θ, R) the model predicts the two-point auto-correlation function ξ_pred(r; Θ, R) of galaxies selected by stellar mass, to be compared with the observed correlation function ξ_obs(r) of an analogously selected galaxy sample.

It is empirically observed that current SAMs do not fit ξ_obs(r) well, and that comparable levels of (mis)match can be obtained by varying either the cosmological parameters Θ or the baryonic recipes R: changing the star-formation law, for example, alters which galaxies satisfy a fixed stellar-mass threshold and thus changes ξ_pred even at fixed Θ, while different choices of Θ can be compensated by different R.

Problem. Determine whether the discrepancy between ξ_pred and ξ_obs in semi-analytic galaxy-formation models is principally attributable to the baryonic recipes R (in particular the star-formation law and feedback prescriptions) or to the assumed cosmological parameters Θ of the underlying dark-matter simulation. Equivalently, identify observables, statistics, or theoretical constraints that break the degeneracy between (Θ, R) so that the cause of the clustering mismatch can be unambiguously assigned.
artifact.status_search_result: The degeneracy between baryonic physics and cosmology in matching galaxy clustering predicted by semi-analytic models remains a known, unresolved issue in galaxy-formation studies. Subsequent work (e.g. on emulators of SAMs, hydrodynamical simulations such as IllustrisTNG and EAGLE, and halo-occupation/SHAM analyses) has explored ways to disentangle baryonic effects from cosmology, but no definitive resolution has been established; the question is generally treated as open.

status_evidence.title: Wang et al. 2008 / subsequent SAM clustering studies
status_evidence.snippet: Similar matches to observed correlation functions can be obtained with different cosmological parameters depending on baryonic recipes.
status_evidence.claim: The cosmology–baryonic-physics degeneracy in SAM clustering predictions has been documented and persists.
